title: Motivation Crowding
hook: The bonus arrives, and the work that felt like care starts feeling like a transaction.
counterintuition: A reward can buy more of a behavior while weakening the reason people wanted to do it. The check is to protect intrinsic motive before adding payment.
tryThisNow: Before adding one reward today, name the existing motive it might replace and the behavior you want after the reward disappears.
keyTakeaway: Pay for what needs payment, but do not price a motive that already belongs to the work.

breakdown.fastRead:
The model card sits on a train delay message desk in Utrecht. Callum's team wants to pay agents per apology sent. The metric looks tidy. The risk is that careful passenger care becomes message volume. Callum marks motivation crowding on the card before the bonus goes live.

Motivation crowding happens when an outside reward changes the reason for acting. A person may start by helping, serving, learning, or taking pride in craft. Add payment in the wrong shape, and the behavior can become a transaction. The old motive gets pushed aside.

A price can replace a purpose.

The correction is to ask what motive is already working. If payment is needed, aim it at support, fairness, or real burden, not at turning care into piecework.
breakdown.deepRead:
The model card on Callum's rail desk defines a proposed score: agents get paid extra for each delay apology sent within two minutes. The goal sounds humane. But the payment may shift attention from passenger clarity to message count. Callum writes intrinsic motive beside the card because many agents already take pride in getting stranded passengers clear information.

Motivation crowding is not a claim that money is bad. People deserve pay. Hard work, risk, expertise, and time should be compensated. The problem is a reward that changes the meaning of the act. A volunteer starts feeling like a contractor. A nurse starts optimizing a count instead of a patient need. A reader returns books for the prize instead of the shared shelf. The reward does not merely add force; it can rewrite the story.

The reward teaches what the act is for.

Hugh sees this in a robotics sensor vendor review. A queue ticket shows engineers voluntarily reporting small sensor defects because they care about reliability. A vendor suggests paying per defect report. Hugh marks intrinsic motive risk on the ticket and asks for protected reporting time instead of a per-report reward.

The question is not whether incentives work. They do. The question is what they work on. If they aim at the wrong surface, they may buy the count while selling off the motive.

Support the motive before you price it.
breakdown.fullRead:
The incident timeline on Maddie's hospital procurement board shows nurses flagging poor glove quality before a large purchase. A finance lead proposes a small payment for every flagged defect. Maddie hears the risk: the payment may turn professional vigilance into a paid errand. She writes payment risk on the timeline before the policy is approved.

Bruno Frey argued for taking intrinsic motivation seriously, including the limits of economic incentives. The point lands in ordinary work: when people already act from duty, craft, loyalty, curiosity, or care, a crude reward can crowd out the internal reason. Payment can still be right, but its design matters. Pay can respect the role, or it can make the role feel bought by the unit.

What would people still do when the reward stops?

You are in an avalanche risk bulletin room in Chamonix with Violet, holding a warranty label from a proposed sponsor. Forecasters already update risky slopes late at night because accuracy matters. The sponsor wants to pay a bonus for each extra bulletin. Violet must decide whether crowding out risk will turn careful warnings into volume. She marks the label and changes the deal to fund overnight staffing, not bulletin count.

Rewards can crowd out civic motives too. A library overdue notice redesign may offer children a prize for every returned book. It took Damon one term to see the press clipping problem: returns rose during the prize weeks, then fell when prizes stopped, and children began asking what they got for bringing books back. Damon marks reward risk and changes the notice toward shared access and amnesty days instead of trinkets.

The best incentive often removes friction instead of buying the act. Pay the overtime. Provide tools. Cover transport. Give public credit. Reduce hassle. Make the wanted behavior easier while leaving its meaning intact. If you must attach a reward, avoid making the smallest visible unit the whole point.

Which motive are you about to replace?

The voting sheet at Catrin's warehouse bonus meeting shows the cost of missing that question. Workers used to help each other clear difficult aisles because the shift ended together. A per-pick bonus made slow aisles feel like someone else's problem. Catrin marks motivation risk and changes the bonus to team completion plus extra staffing for hard aisles.

Pay for what needs payment, but do not price a motive that already belongs to the work.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Motivation crowding shows that rewards can change the meaning of a behavior. Readers need to protect existing motives before adding payment or prizes.

reviewCards.front: Before adding a reward, what should you identify?
reviewCards.back: Identify the motive already driving the behavior and whether the reward could replace it.
It can make the visible count the point and crowd out care, craft, duty, or shared ownership.

reviewCards.front: What is often better than buying the act?
reviewCards.back: Remove friction: time, tools, staffing, transport, respect, or simpler process.

reviewCards.front: Does motivation crowding mean money is bad?
reviewCards.back: No. It means incentive design can change the meaning of the work.

reviewCards.front: What is the core correction for motivation crowding?
reviewCards.back: Pay for what needs payment, but do not price a motive that already belongs to the work.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to add support or payment without replacing the intrinsic motive that already drives a useful behavior.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a reward targets a count, then I will ask what motive or quality the count may crowd out.
If people already contribute from care, then I will remove friction before adding prizes.
If a safety behavior is proposed for per-unit pay, then I will protect time and staffing first.
If individual bonuses weaken cooperation, then I will redesign around shared completion.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, inspect one proposed reward and write the existing motive it might replace.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, redesign one incentive so it removes friction or rewards the broader outcome, not the smallest count.
